topics.title: What data science is
topics.technical: Data science extracts decisions from data by combining statistics, programming and domain knowledge: framing a question, gathering and cleaning data, modelling it, and communicating a result someone acts on. It is a pipeline, and every stage can sink the answer.
topics.simple: Turning messy real-world data into decisions someone can trust and act on.

topics.title: Python and the data stack
topics.technical: NumPy vectorises numeric arrays, pandas handles labelled tables, and Jupyter notebooks host the experiment-first workflow. Vectorised thinking — operate on whole columns, not element loops — is the productivity unlock.
topics.simple: The daily tools: fast arrays, smart tables, and notebooks where code and charts sit together.

topics.title: Loading and cleaning data
topics.technical: Real data arrives dirty: missing values, wrong types, duplicates, inconsistent categories. pandas reads CSV/JSON/SQL, and cleaning — imputation, type coercion, deduplication — typically consumes most of a project's hours.
topics.simple: Most of the job is scrubbing data into a state you can actually analyse.

topics.title: Exploratory data analysis
topics.technical: EDA interrogates data before modelling: distributions, correlations, outliers and group differences, seen through summaries and plots. Its purpose is to form hypotheses and catch problems the numbers alone hide.
topics.simple: Look at the data from every angle first — its shape tells you what to ask.

topics.title: Descriptive statistics
topics.technical: Mean, median, variance and quantiles summarise a distribution; each hides something, so you report several. Skew, spread and outliers change which summary is honest — the average income of ten people and a billionaire is a lie.
topics.simple: Numbers that describe a pile of data — and knowing when the average deceives.

topics.title: Data visualisation
topics.technical: matplotlib and seaborn turn numbers into charts chosen to fit the question: distributions, relationships, comparisons, trends. The chart's job is to make the reader's conclusion inevitable and honest.
topics.simple: Pick the right chart so the reader sees the truth at a glance.

topics.title: Probability foundations
topics.technical: Probability quantifies uncertainty: distributions, independence, conditional probability and Bayes' rule. It underlies every model's claim and every A/B test's verdict.
topics.simple: The math of chance — how likely, given what we already know.

topics.title: Statistical inference
topics.technical: Inference reasons from a sample to a population: confidence intervals bound estimates, hypothesis tests weigh evidence, and p-values are misread more than any number in science. Effect size matters more than significance.
topics.simple: Drawing careful conclusions about everyone from data about some.

topics.title: Hypothesis testing and A/B tests
topics.technical: A/B testing compares variants with a test statistic and a pre-registered threshold; peeking, multiple comparisons and underpowered samples are the classic ways to fool yourself. Randomisation is what licenses the causal claim.
topics.simple: The disciplined way to decide if a change actually helped, not just looked like it did.

topics.title: SQL for analysis
topics.technical: Most data lives in relational databases; SQL selects, filters, joins, groups and windows it at the source, before it ever reaches Python. An analyst who cannot join tables is stranded.
topics.simple: Ask databases precise questions and get exactly the rows you need.

topics.title: Feature engineering
topics.technical: Models see features, not reality: encode categories, scale numerics, extract time components, and combine variables that interact. Good features routinely beat fancier algorithms on tabular data.
topics.simple: Translating raw facts into the signals a model can actually learn from.

topics.title: Regression modelling
topics.technical: Linear and regularised regression predict numbers and, crucially, explain them through coefficients. Assumptions — linearity, independence, constant variance — decide whether the explanation is real.
topics.simple: Predicting a number and reading which inputs drive it.

topics.title: Classification modelling
topics.technical: Logistic regression, trees and ensembles predict categories; precision, recall and the confusion matrix measure them honestly under imbalance. The threshold is a business decision.
topics.simple: Sorting records into classes, and measuring it without fooling yourself.

topics.title: Model validation
topics.technical: Train/validation/test splits and cross-validation estimate performance on unseen data; leakage and overfitting are the twin enemies. You tune on validation and touch test exactly once.
topics.simple: Proving a model works on data it has never seen — the only score that counts.

topics.title: Clustering and dimensionality
topics.technical: k-means and hierarchical clustering find groups; PCA compresses many correlated features into a few informative ones. Both explore and simplify rather than predict.
topics.simple: Finding natural groups and shrinking wide data down to what matters.

topics.title: Time series
topics.technical: Temporal data breaks the independence assumption: trend, seasonality and autocorrelation demand their own methods, and you must never shuffle the past into the future when validating.
topics.simple: Data that arrives in order — where yesterday predicts tomorrow and you must not peek ahead.

topics.title: Machine learning pipelines
topics.technical: scikit-learn Pipelines chain preprocessing and models into one fitted object, so the same transforms apply to train and production alike — the antidote to leakage and to 'works in the notebook only'.
topics.simple: Wrapping cleaning and modelling into one repeatable unit that behaves the same everywhere.

topics.title: Communicating results
topics.technical: A result nobody understands changes nothing: dashboards, clear visuals and a narrative that states the decision, the confidence and the caveats turn analysis into action. This is the half that gets analysts promoted.
topics.simple: Telling the story of what the data means so someone actually acts on it.

topics.title: Ethics and pitfalls
topics.technical: Correlation is not causation, samples carry bias, and Simpson's paradox flips conclusions on aggregation. Privacy law and fairness constrain what you may collect and conclude — mistakes here are expensive.
topics.simple: The traps that turn confident analysis into confident nonsense — and the duty to avoid them.

topics.title: Reproducibility and tooling
topics.technical: Version data, code and environment; notebooks that only you can run are not results. Git, environments and documented steps let a colleague rerun and trust your work.
topics.simple: Making your analysis something another person can rerun and believe.

topics.title: The capstone
topics.technical: Take one real dataset end to end: question, clean, explore, model with honest validation, and present a decision with its uncertainty. A finished, documented analysis is the portfolio piece.
topics.simple: One complete project — question to defended conclusion — that you can show.
